spatial_claims.claim: C lies on segment AB between A and B, with AC > CB (AC is the greater segment of the extreme and mean ratio cut)
D lies on segment AB between A and B, with AD = DB = AB/2 (D is the midpoint)
Since AC > AB/2 = AD, the ordering on segment AB is A-D-C-B

configuration_map: All points lie on a single line segment AB. Point D is the midpoint of AB (AD = DB). Point C is the golden ratio cut point with AC > CB, so AC > AB/2 = AD, giving the linear order A—D—C—B. No other geometric figures (triangles, circles, angles) are constructed. The proof operates entirely on algebraic relationships among lengths and areas (squares and rectangles) of sub-segments of AB. The quantity (AC + AD) is treated as a pure length for algebraic expansion, not as a constructed segment with a new endpoint.
pass_reason: The proof is essentially algebraic, manipulating squares and rectangles of line segments using Propositions 2.1, 2.4, and 6.17. The only spatial claims are that C and D both lie on segment AB in the order A-D-C-B, which is trivially consistent. There are no angle decompositions, no interior/exterior point arguments, no ray orderings, and no circle arguments — nothing that could create a spatial configuration contradiction.
